summary:
The design is sound in outline. It builds the tree only from the finished ScanResult.Store, which avoids both no-go spikes, and it uses the stock TreeView setup that was measured. I found no blockers and 12 things to fix (5 major, 7 minor).

Major:
- One standard key hangs the window and blows the memory budget. On a WPF TreeView, the numpad '*' key expands every folder below the selected one. The design's memory argument assumes a person opens big folders one at a time by hand.
- The one-store-in-memory rule (the design's only unproven precondition) depends on every place that holds scan data being cleared. The release test never selects a row, and the TreeView is reported to keep a reference to the selected item.
- The hook requires case A's rows to be on screen but never scrolls them into view.
- Three required test cases have no test setup or hook step: a parent of size 0, rounding of shares, and expand state kept after scrolling.
- If row 5 misses 0.5 s, the planned fallback (sorting on a worker thread) does not shorten the time that row 5 measures.

Minor: the share bar's width is checked from the data object, not from what is drawn. Exceptions thrown while expanding a folder are swallowed silently. The rounding rule for one decimal place is not specified. Sparse and compressed test files do not have a size known in advance. Both regex rules have gaps. Case B and the responsiveness check (StallRig) need tighter setups.

Sources checked: the KB938416 claim (recalled) supports the decision to implement INotifyPropertyChanged. Both the '*' key and the selected-item leak have sources outside this repo. The cited prior art (FolderSizes, FreeSize) was cut off in the design text, and the design does not rely on it.

findings.claim: A standard WPF TreeView key defeats both the memory bound and the responsiveness argument. The numpad '*' key on a TreeViewItem expands everything below it. On a drive root, that sets IsExpanded=true on every folder. Each one runs ChildrenLargestFirst and builds a node array synchronously on the UI thread, and the recursive expand generates a container for every item. For a 5M-entry store, that means millions of FolderTreeNodes kept 'until the next scan' on top of the 652 MiB store (about 208 MiB of headroom). It also means seconds to minutes with no message pumping, so Windows shows 'Not Responding'. The design's key decision on lazy children says 'The worst case is bounded by how many big folders one person opens by hand'. That is false: one keystroke opens all of them.
findings.evidence: key_decisions: 'Children load lazily ... The worst case is bounded by how many big folders one person opens by hand, against about 208 MiB of headroom (816 of 1024 MiB)'. Sources: https://github.com/microsoft/microsoft-ui-xaml/issues/9924 ('The TreeView controls in WPF ... allow ... asterisk key: recursively expand all child nodes') and https://stackoverflow.com/questions/24150966 ('the asterisks triggers an action in the treeview by default').
findings.fix: Handle PreviewKeyDown on FolderTree and mark Key.Multiply as handled (or override it in a TreeViewItem subclass). Add a case to hook tree mode: send Key.Multiply to a selected root row on case B's tree and assert that no folder beyond the root was expanded.

findings.claim: The design's one unproven precondition (the old store is released before the next scan) depends on remembering to clear every reference, not on how the code is built. StartScan clears FolderTree.ItemsSource and 'MainWindow fields', and the release test checks only that. Several other things can keep a 650 MiB store alive. (1) TreeView.SelectedItem and the focused TreeViewItem: a person clicks a row before picking a new folder, and WPF TreeView has been reported to keep the selected view-model strongly after it leaves the items. (2) The other result-bound lists the ending already fills from ScanResult.Store (LargestFiles.Top at ~:422, unreadable paths at ~:378), if their rows carry the store. (3) Lambdas in the ending block that capture the result. The FSA_HOOK_RELEASE case never selects or focuses a row, so it passes on a path no person takes. If the precondition fails, two stores coexist during the next scan (about 1.3 GiB at 5M entries), which breaches the U-001 budget. The release check also has a known false-failure trap: in tier-0 JIT, a local holding the store stays live until the method ends.
findings.evidence: Window wiring: 'make sure no MainWindow field still references the previous ScanResult'. Hook tree mode: 'FSA_HOOK_RELEASE ... captur[es] a WeakReference to the first store, forces GC'. The case for starting a second scan does not select a row. TreeView selected-item leak: https://stackoverflow.com/questions/12722813 ('When I select an item in the TreeView, the corresponding bound ViewModel is strongly hold ... not released when the ViewModel is removed').
findings.fix: Make the leak harmless by construction. FolderTreeNode holds a small TreeSession object (not the ScanStore), and StartScan calls session.Close(), which nulls the store. Any node retained by a WPF internal (SelectedItem, recycled container, automation peer) then retains a few bytes, not the store. Route every other store-derived list through one ShownScan holder that StartScan clears. In the release case, select and focus a depth-3 row first, then trigger the new scan, wait for a ContextIdle dispatcher pass, and take the WeakReference in a [MethodImpl(NoInlining)] helper.

findings.claim: Tree mode walks breadth-first to depth 4, expanding every folder, and 'A row that is not realized in case A fails the case'. The design never says how off-screen rows get realized. Fully expanded, case A has a 4-level tree plus a junction, a symlink, a sparse sibling, an empty folder, a subfolder chain and the special-character names, which is easily more rows than the tree's star-sized cell shows. That cell shares the window with the picker, the outcome panel and the largest-files list. With IsVirtualizing and Recycling, rows outside the viewport have no container, so ContainerFromItem returns null. As designed, case A fails whenever the tree is taller than the viewport, or the builder has to invent the scroll logic with no contract for it. Microsoft's own guidance says virtualized TreeView items must be brought into view through the panel before their container exists.
findings.evidence: FSA_HOOK_MODE=tree log contract: 'rendered:{...}|null' and error_cases 'a case-A row is not realized'. Hook responsibility: 'walks FolderTree breadth-first to depth 4, expanding each folder'. https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/desktop/wpf/controls/how-to-find-a-treeviewitem-in-a-treeview ('In the case where items might be virtualized, you also must realize a TreeViewItem').
findings.fix: Add a step to the hook contract: for each row, call VirtualizingPanel.BringIndexIntoViewPublic(index) on the parent's items host, wait for a Loaded-priority dispatcher pass, then read the container, before moving to the next row, because Recycling reuses containers. Or set the window's size for case A so the fully expanded tree fits, and record the row count it is sized for.

findings.claim: Three cases the design marks as material have no test setup or hook step to exercise them. (a) 'show a share of a zero parent (row 3)' needs a folder with rolled on-disk 0 that has children. Case A's files are 'distinct whole multiples of 4 KiB (at least 4 KiB)', so it contains no empty files. Case B's 100k folder has 50 nonzero files, so its parent is not 0, and case B runs in FSA_HOOK_EXPAND mode, which logs only timings, not rows. (b) 'format a share to one decimal' needs 1/3, 2/3 and a nonzero share that rounds to 0.0 % (a 4 KiB child under a parent of at least 8 MiB). Case A's shape guarantees none of these. (c) 'keep expand state through recycling' needs a scroll away and back, plus a collapse and re-expand of the parent. No hook mode scrolls, so tree mode, FSA_HOOK_EXPAND and FSA_HOOK_RELEASE all miss it.
findings.evidence: cases: 'show a share of a zero parent', 'format a share to one decimal', 'keep expand state through recycling and re-expansion'. Window cases: 'Case A: a 4-level temp tree whose files are distinct whole multiples of 4 KiB (at least 4 KiB)...'. Hook contract lists only tree / EXPAND / RELEASE behaviours.
findings.fix: Add to case A: a folder of three 0-byte files (zero parent); a parent of exactly three equal 4 KiB children (1/3) and one of 4 KiB + 8 KiB (1/3, 2/3); and a folder at least 8 MiB holding one 4 KiB file (rounds to 0.0 %). Add an FSA_HOOK_RECYCLE step: expand one child low in a folder with more rows than fit on screen, scroll to the end and back, collapse and re-expand the parent, then log which rows are expanded and in what order.

findings.claim: The only contingency for row 5 does not address row 5's metric. Row 5 times 'from expanding it in the app to its first screen of children being drawn'. Moving ChildrenLargestFirst to a worker and returning the Children swap to the dispatcher leaves the sort and the node build inside that same interval. It only frees the UI thread while the person waits. So if row 5 misses 0.5 s, the builder applies the named fix, row 5 still fails, and the decision the design itself rates 'expensive' (stock TreeView) is reopened with no plan. The risk is real: the design asserts every one of 5 opens, but U-001 reported only a 230 ms median from a framework-dependent exe, not the tail or the published single-file build.
findings.evidence: key_decisions: 'If row 5 misses 0.5 s, the sort moves to a worker and the Children swap returns to the dispatcher.' Owed row 5 check: 'the time from expanding it in the app to its first screen of children being drawn'. U-001: 'cold expand 230 ms median'.
findings.fix: Have the hook log how open 1 splits into sort, node build and container generation. Name a remedy that shortens the measured interval: build FolderTreeNodes only for the indices WPF actually asks for (a lazy read-only IList over the ChildRow[]), so node build scales with the screen, not with 100k. Keep 'worker' only as a responsiveness measure, and say so.

findings.claim: Row 3's bar is checked from the node, not from what is drawn. That is the silent-binding hole the design's change (1) was meant to close. The hook contract's 'rendered' object holds {name,onDisk,size,share}, and barWidth is logged only as a node property. If the bar's Width binding has a wrong path or type, the bar draws at zero width and every check still passes. The contract also does not say how the hook tells the TextBlocks apart.
findings.evidence: FSA_HOOK_MODE=tree log: '..., barWidth, rendered:{name,onDisk,size,share}|null'. Row 3: 'as a bar and a percentage'.
findings.fix: Give each template element an x:Name (NameText, OnDiskText, SizeText, ShareText, ShareBar). The hook finds them with FindName through the container's ContentPresenter and logs rendered.barActualWidth. Case A asserts it within 1 px of Share × track width.

findings.claim: The rounding rule for one decimal place is never stated. The contract says only that 'The formatter must round the way the test expects'. Test files are 4 KiB multiples, so shares with power-of-two denominators give exact binary midpoints (1 of 16 units = 6.25 %, 3 of 16 = 18.75 %). At those values the PowerShell check and the app can disagree. PowerShell's [math]::Round(x,1) rounds half to even. .NET's 'F1' formatting of doubles has documented and disputed midpoint behaviour. The row 3 check then fails or passes depending on which one each side happened to use.
findings.evidence: FolderTreeRowText: 'the share as Share*100 to one decimal place'. Case: 'The formatter must round the way the test expects'. https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.math.round?view=net-10.0 (Round(Double, Int32) 'rounds midpoint values to the nearest even number'). https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/issues/1640 and https://github.com/dotnet/docs/issues/22089 (format-string midpoint rounding inconsistent).
findings.fix: Fix the rule in the contract: Math.Round(Share*100, 1, MidpointRounding.AwayFromZero).ToString('F1', culture). WindowCases.ps1 computes the expected value with [math]::Round(x, 1, [MidpointRounding]::AwayFromZero). Add a 1/16 share to case A.

findings.claim: The sparse or compressed sibling in case A has no known on-disk size, but rows 2 to 4 are checked 'on a temp tree with known sizes'. NTFS allocates sparse and compressed files in compression units (16 clusters, 64 KiB at 4 KiB clusters), so a sparse file with 4 KiB written takes 64 KiB on disk. An NTFS-compressed file's allocation depends on its content. The sibling's on-disk size also flows into every ancestor total and share on its path. So an expected value hand-computed from the bytes written is wrong in a way that depends on the file system.
findings.evidence: Case A: 'a sparse or NTFS-compressed sibling'. Row 2 check: 'On a temp tree with known sizes'. https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/archive/blogs/ntdebugging/understanding-ntfs-compression ('The default size of the CU is 16 clusters'). https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/answers/questions/1459700 ('I had to write at least 64KB of 0 to see the size of the file reflect a sparse').
findings.fix: Use a sparse file only (not compressed), with data written at 64 KiB-aligned ranges. After creating it, read its on-disk size with GetCompressedFileSize (or fsutil) inside WindowCases.ps1 and compute the expected ancestor totals and shares from the measured value. Also require sibling folder totals to be distinct, not only file sizes, so the entry-order tie-break never decides the expected order.

findings.claim: Expansion does real work (ChildrenLargestFirst plus the node build) inside FolderTreeNode.IsExpanded's setter, reached through a TwoWay binding. WPF catches exceptions thrown by a source setter during a TwoWay update and turns them into a 'Data Error 8' trace line. So a store fault on expand never reaches the app's failure path. The person sees an expanded folder that shows only the blank placeholder row, and the placeholder's store-reading getters may also throw into the same trace.
findings.evidence: FolderTreeNode: 'On the first IsExpanded=true it calls store.ChildrenLargestFirst(entry)'. The ItemContainerStyle 'binds TreeViewItem.IsExpanded TwoWay'. https://github.com/elmish/Elmish.WPF/issues/10 ('System.Windows.Data Error: 8 : Cannot save value from target back to source ... InvalidOperationException').
findings.fix: Keep the setter trivial. Do the load in a TreeViewItem.Expanded handler on FolderTree, which is a bubbling routed event in code-behind, calling node.EnsureChildren(), where exceptions reach the dispatcher's unhandled-exception path. Or catch the exception in the setter and send it to the window's existing failure handling. Make the placeholder's getters return constants.

findings.claim: The rule 'Core does not publish a live ScanStore' misses most of the ways a store would actually be published. The regex needs the pattern 'ScanStore <space> Name {|;|=>'. It does not match a nullable 'public ScanStore? Live { get; }', a method 'public ScanStore Live() =>', a positional record parameter 'record ScanProgress(..., ScanStore Store)' (the most natural place, since ScanProgress already carries TopLevel mid-scan), or 'event Action<ScanStore>'. The design dropped the static-field rule for being 'easily dodged', and this one is equally dodged. The rule guards the design's central premise.
findings.evidence: architecture_rules[1].must_not_match: 'public[ \t]+[^;(){}=]*\bScanStore\b[ \t]+\w+[ \t]*(\{|;|=>)'. The coherence check explains dropping the static-field regex because 'the regex is easily dodged'.
findings.fix: Turn it into an allow-list. Over src/FsAnalyser.Core/**, except the store's own files (Store/ScanStore*.cs), the scanner file that holds the private _store, and ScanResult.cs, forbid '\bScanStore\b' outright. Then any new mention of the type outside those files fails and has to be justified.

findings.claim: The rule 'never re-sorts' covers only src/FsAnalyser.App/FolderTree*.cs. The easiest way to break it is a CollectionViewSource/SortDescriptions in MainWindow.xaml, or FolderTree.Items.SortDescriptions in MainWindow.xaml.cs, where the tree actually lives and is wired. Neither file is covered. 'There is no CollectionViewSource and no view-side sorting' holds only as long as the builder remembers it.
findings.evidence: architecture_rules[0].files: 'src/FsAnalyser.App/FolderTree*.cs'. FolderTree component: lives_at 'src/FsAnalyser.App/MainWindow.xaml' ('There is no CollectionViewSource and no view-side sorting').
findings.fix: Add a rule over src/FsAnalyser.App/*.xaml and MainWindow.xaml.cs that forbids 'SortDescriptions|CollectionViewSource|IsLiveSorting'. First check that the flat list's existing bytes sort (~:302-307) does not use them. If it does, move that sort into the row-building code.

findings.claim: Case B's timing is not what its 'cold' label says. The wiring expands the root at completion, which already JIT-compiles ChildrenLargestFirst and the node build, so open 1 does not include JIT. If FSA_HOOK_EXPAND points at the scan root itself, the real cold open happens untimed in the completion handler and all five timed opens are warm re-opens. Separately, case 13's shape (a new scan started over a large shown tree, plus the completion hand-off) is sent to 'the existing StallRig responsiveness case re-run'. That case predates the tree and does not drive either step.
findings.evidence: Window cases: 'Case B: a temp folder of 100,000 files ... driven with FSA_HOOK_EXPAND'. Window wiring: 'build the root node ... expand it'. Case D: 'the existing StallRig responsiveness case re-run on this build for row 6'. Case 'keep the window responsive' shape: '... then the completion hand-off, then a new scan starting over a large shown tree'.
findings.fix: Require the 100k folder to be a child of the scan root, never the root. The hook logs an error if FSA_HOOK_EXPAND resolves to the root. Drop 'JIT' from the meaning of cold. Extend StallRig's script to finish a scan with the 100k folder expanded and then start a second scan, sampling the heartbeat across both steps.

dimensions_checked.result: M5: the worker-thread fallback does not shorten the interval row 5 measures. m3: sparse and compressed files have no on-disk size known in advance (NTFS allocates in 64 KiB units). M1 also refutes the assumption that the worst case is 'opened by hand'. Checked and holding: KB938416 (recalled) backs the INotifyPropertyChanged decision. The KB's strict condition does not match, but the general PropertyDescriptor retention it describes does (betaarchive KB mirror; dotnet/wpf#11236).

M1: numpad '*' expands everything below a row, which breaks the memory bound and keeps the window busy for a long time. Also checked: an empty folder, links, a parent of size 0, '_' and '&' in names, a cancelled or failed ending, a second scan. The design covers these as behaviours.

M2: releasing the old store depends on remembering to clear every reference (MainWindow fields, the TreeView's selected item, other lists built from the result, captured lambdas). An indirection (the TreeSession / ShownScan holders) makes a leak harmless.
none: the only extras are the Core-side rule in an App-only slice (cheap, and it guards the design's premise) and FolderTreeRowText as its own class (a matter of taste, already left open).

m2: the midpoint rounding rule for one decimal place is unspecified, and PowerShell's [math]::Round defaults to round-half-even. The hook's way of telling the TextBlocks apart is unspecified (folded into m1's fix).
m4: the expansion work runs in a setter reached through a TwoWay binding, and WPF swallows exceptions there as 'Data Error 8'. Cancel and failure endings are covered by the existing hook modes.

none: every owed row (1-6) is served. Keeping TopLevelTracker and not publishing the store go against what the SL-042 and SL-039 docs expected, but the design says so openly and records both in the SL-044 design note. The design stays on App code and the hook, and does not rebuild C1 or C2.
m5: the Core publish rule's regex misses nullable types, methods, record parameters and events. m6: the no-sort rule does not cover MainWindow.xaml or MainWindow.xaml.cs, where the tree lives.

M3: the hook never scrolls off-screen rows into view, so case A's 'fail if not realized' rule fires on any tree taller than the viewport. M4: three material cases (a parent of size 0, rounding, expand state after recycling) have no test setup or hook step. m1: the bar is checked from the node, not from what is drawn. m7: case B's 'cold' label and StallRig's shape. Settling M3 and M4 means running tests/window/WindowCases.ps1 case A against a built tree. That can only happen after the build.

none: the change is in-process and read-only over a finished store. The hook log lists only the test's own temp tree, and the report keeps schema 1 with no listing, as Q-016 requires. The shipped exe already honoured DOTNET_STARTUP_HOOKS before this slice, and that stays within the same user's trust.
